Mentoring notes, Hansa, 12 March.
Today I suggested Arohi spend six months in a big agency before going freelance, the way we all did. She went quiet, turned her pen over twice, and said, 'Can I disagree? I think that path worked a decade back. Most studios I talk to now hire from small online case studies, and I already have three clients.' She apologised twice while saying it, and her voice was careful, as though she was afraid of seeming ungrateful. My first reaction was to defend my advice. I stopped myself and asked her to show me the clients' work. She was right about most of it.
Next session: she leads, I ask questions. I told her the disagreement was the most useful thing she's said all year.

qa.q: How many clients does Arohi already have?
qa.a: She already has three clients.

qa.q: Why did Arohi apologise twice while disagreeing?
qa.a: She felt loyal to Hansa and worried about seeming ungrateful, even while doubting the advice, so her courage came wrapped in care.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that let the disagreement help rather than hurt?
qa.a: Hansa held back the urge to defend, asked to see the clients' work and admitted Arohi was mostly right, which is the humility this stage needs.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Arohi disagreed with the advice?
qa.a: Hansa's first reaction was defensive, but Hansa chose to look at the clients' work and ended up valuing the disagreement as the most useful thing all year.

grounding: A mentor's notes show a young woman respectfully disagreeing with advice based on how the industry used to work, and the mentor choosing to listen.

Thursday night.
Tenzin said again today that I should build the launch around trade fairs and printed brochures. 'That's how I built my whole client list.' And I nodded. Again.
The thing is, he built it ten years ago. Our buyers now find us through short videos and online groups; I have last quarter's numbers.
I owe him so much. I'm not the girl who says 'sorry, small point' any more, and that's because of him. That's what makes this hard. Disagreeing feels like ingratitude. But staying quiet would be pretending.
Tomorrow I'll say it: 'I think the fairs matter less now. Can I show you why?' Calm voice, numbers ready.
If he gets annoyed, he gets annoyed. I really hope he doesn't.
- Binita

"Trisha, you should send your pitch to the magazines first," Yamini said. "That's how I got my first break."
"Mm." Trisha stirred her coffee.
"Mm? What does 'mm' mean?"
"It means... can I disagree a little?"

Yamini was quiet. Trisha's heart was thumping. She owed Yamini so much.
"I didn't know that," Yamini said at last. "Show me your newsletter."
Trisha let out her breath and pulled up her phone.

I remember sitting across from Mridul sir in his office, holding a printout of his advice. "Get a government job first, then think about startups," he'd said. Ten years ago, that was wise. He'd done it himself.
I admired him so much. He had taught me half of what I knew. That's what made it hard. Because I didn't agree. In my field now, startups hire freshers, and the government exams I'd need would take two years.
I said, "Sir, I think the industry has changed. Can I explain why?" My voice was smaller than I wanted.
He listened. He frowned. Then he said, "You may be right, beti. I haven't hired anyone in years." I'm Ayesha, and that was the day I stopped being only his student.

qa.q: What had Mridul sir advised Ayesha to do first?
qa.a: Get a government job first, then think about startups.

qa.q: Why was it hard for Ayesha to disagree?
qa.a: She admired Mridul sir and felt loyal and grateful, so doubting his advice made her nervous, her voice smaller than she wanted.

qa.q: What went well in how Ayesha raised her disagreement?
qa.a: She asked respectfully if she could explain and gave reasons about how the field had changed.

qa.q: How does Mridul sir see the disagreement once he listens?
qa.a: He seems surprised but humble enough to admit he may be out of touch, since he hasn't hired anyone in years.

Mentoring journal, Thursday
I suggested to Trisha that she build her client list the way I did: cold calls and printed brochures. She nodded, and then she didn't do it. Today she came in with a folder and said, "Can I be honest? I don't think brochures work in this market any more." She showed me how her clients find her through short videos and referrals. Her hands were tight on the folder, and she kept adding "with respect" and "you taught me so much". I could see how torn she was. My first instinct was to defend my way. I didn't. I asked her to teach me how the videos work. We have agreed that she will lead the next workshop on it.
Pradeep

qa.a: Cold calls and printed brochures.

qa.a: She felt torn, loyal and grateful to Pradeep but doubtful about the advice, and nervous about saying so.

qa.a: Pradeep resisted defending the old way and asked Trisha to teach the videos, and she will lead the next workshop.

qa.a: Trisha might have stopped being honest and quietly drifted away from the mentoring.

Sunday
On Friday Kalyani Ma'am told me again to stay off online platforms and let my portfolio speak "the old way": a printed book, agency visits, patience. Ten years ago that's how she got her first big client, and I love that story. But nearly every studio I've spoken to this year found its designers through their online work. I didn't say anything. I nodded, like always.
Tonight I feel torn. She's the reason I'm a designer at all; she spent Saturdays reviewing my sketches when nobody else would. Disagreeing feels almost like betrayal. But following advice I don't believe in isn't loyalty either.
I'm going to say it on Tuesday, carefully: "Ma'am, I think the industry has changed here. Can I show you what I'm seeing?" If she's the person I think she is, she'll listen.
Rajni
